Type 2 moves only increase the sum of the products of the pairs. The sum is increased by . This is equivalent to , which is clearly nonnegative since and .

Remarks (added by pf02, November 2025)[edit]

The first solution can not be called a solution. There are several issues with it. The first issue is that the notion of "pairing" is not defined. The notions "type 1 move" vs. "type 2 move" are defined only very loosely. The way they are used contradicts the fact that they are meant to be complementary. Indeed, we can not assume we have only strict inequalities among the 's and the 's.

The second issue is with the last paragraph. Consider the sentences "Suppose that is the biggest -value that is not paired with its -value in the and pairing. Then, switch this -value with the -value currently paired with ." These two sentences do not make sense. Furthermore, depending on what meaning we would want to force on these two sentences, and on what "type 2 move" may mean, the sentence which follows, "This is obviously a type 2 move" may or may not be true. And finally, the sentence "Continue this process until you reach back to the - pairing" is unclear: it is not clear that we would reach "the - pairing" (whatever "pairing" may mean).

Solution 2 is incorrect. The author assumed that and are terms in , but this is not true unless and .

(Never mind the fact that there is a crucial sentence which does not make sense: "assume, for contradiction, that neither of those conditions are true and that there exists some order of s that are not ordered in the form such that is at a maximum out of all possible permutations and is greater than the sum ". But a benign and eager reader can guess what the author most likely wanted to express in this sentence.)

The remark which follows the two "solutions" makes no sense at all.

Below I will give a solution to the problem.

For example if we swap and in the set (or sequence) , the new set (or sequence) will be . This way, each element in the permuted set has a precisely defined index.

We will call a transposition if it swaps two nearby (or neighboring) elements of . In other words is adjacent, if it permutes into . We will call a transposition if given and the elements being swapped, the inequality is satisfied.

This is a little more complicated. We will prove it by induction. First, notice that the statement is true for .

Let us verify that all this can be done using positive, adjacent transpositions. The case when we don't move , but only permute follows immediately from the induction assumption. In terms of positions in the sequence has now to the left, and to the right. Now make another transposition. Continue this process till is at position , followed by . We can now apply the induction hypothesis to this sequence of non-increasing numbers.

This concludes the proof of lemma 2, and of the problem.
